synopsis: Existing standards cover collision avoidance, automatic intervention, control-system hardware and software, and environmental qualification, and provide scenario vocabulary, but they become binding only through legal incorporation or other applicable conformity and contractual routes; South Africa's braking mandate preceded a validation standard [f830, f315, f2062, f2144, f11458]. Heavy-machinery standards accept simulation as one verification method, but no off-road clause accepting it as a replacement for the physical tests discussed was found; the full paid texts were unavailable, so this is not evidence that replacement is prohibited [f9456, f7739]. The reviewed standards do not define simulation-credibility acceptance or prescribe testing quantities: gaps include detection and false-alarm sample sizes, required virtual job-site counts, and a published ISO rule validating a machine family from N representative machines [f5110, f5154, f5160, f11933, f6683]. Survey capture is the only environment-creation method identified whose geometric accuracy can be measured against a published standard, whereas no standard or regulator-endorsed method was found by October 2026 treating ordinary generative weather or lighting edits as physically equivalent safety-critical sensor evidence [f78, f3719, f4910]. The booklet labels standards unissued by October 2026 as draft, under publication or under revision, and several ISO parts were due to change in late 2026; a 2027 programme should therefore use actual published editions and maintain an agreed baseline with change control rather than freeze the October snapshot [f46, f11913, f1161, f11914, f11222]. Applicability to the specific machine, jurisdiction and safety function remains unresolved and should be an early specialist-confirmed gate; no standard guarantees that a first-time simulation organization can meet a four-month validation schedule [f9786, f9787, f7594].
